Al-Shafi’i said: It is permissible for the pilgrim to kill everything whose meat is not eaten, and there is no difference between young and old ones. He made the general reason that they are not eaten. Abu Hanifa said: The pilgrim must kill the rabid dog and the wolf, because they are wild dogs. If he kills something other than them, he must pay its ransom, unless another wild beast attacks it and kills it, in which case he does not have to pay ransom. This is the opinion of Al-Awza’i and Al-Hasan ibn Salih ibn Hayy. Zafar ibn Al-Hudhayl said: He must pay ransom for anything other than that, even if it attacks him. Some people said: What is meant by the crow here is the spotted crow, which is the one with white on its belly and back but not on its armor, which is black, and the a’sam, which is the white, based on what was narrated by An-Nasa’i on the authority of Amr ibn Ali Al-Fallas, on the authority of Yahya Al-Qattan, on the authority of Shu’bah, on the authority of Qatadah, on the authority of Sa’id ibn Al-Musayyab, on the authority of Aishah, on the authority of the Prophet, may God bless him and grant him peace, who said: “There are five things that a person in ihram may kill: a snake, a mouse, a kite, a spotted crow, and a rabid dog.” The majority are of the opinion that what is meant by it is more general than that, based on what was proven in the two Sahihs of its general wording. Malik, may God have mercy on him, said: A person in ihram may not kill a crow unless it attacks him and harms him. Mujahid ibn Jabr and a group said: He should not kill it, but rather throw it away. The same was narrated on the authority of Ali. Hisham narrated: Yazid ibn Abi Ziyad told us, on the authority of Abd Al-Rahman ibn Abi Na’im, on the authority of Abu Sa’id, on the authority of the Prophet, may God bless him and grant him peace, that he was asked about what a person in ihram may kill? He said: The snake, the scorpion, the mousetrap, the crow that shoots but does not kill it, the rabid dog, the kite, and the wild beast. Narrated by Abu Dawud on the authority of Ahmad ibn Hanbal, and al-Tirmidhi on the authority of Ahmad ibn Mani’, both on the authority of Hisham, and Ibn Majah on the authority of Abu Karim and on the authority of Muhammad ibn Fadil, both on the authority of Yazid ibn Abi Ziyad, and it is weak because of it. Al-Tirmidhi said: This is a good hadith. And the Almighty said: And whoever among you kills it intentionally, the penalty is an equivalent of what he killed from livestock. Ibn Abi Hatim said: Abu Saeed Al-Ashj narrated to us, Ibn Ulayyah narrated to us from Ayoub, who said: I was told from Tawus that he said: The penalty is not imposed on the one who kills game by mistake, rather the penalty is imposed on the one who kills it deliberately. This is a strange opinion from Tawus, and he adheres to the apparent meaning of the verse. Mujahid bin Jabr said: What is meant by the intentional here is the one who intends to kill the game, forgetting his state of ihram. As for the one who intentionally kills the game while remembering his state of ihram, then his matter is greater than that he should make expiation, and his state of ihram is invalidated. Ibn Jarir narrated it from him through the chain of transmission of Ibn Abi Nujayh, Layth bin Abi Sulaym and others from him, and it is also a strange opinion. What the majority are of the opinion is that the one who kills intentionally and the one who forgets are equal in the obligation of the penalty upon him. Al-Zuhri said: The Book indicates the deliberate one, and the Sunnah indicates the forgetful one. The meaning of this is that the Qur’an indicates the necessity of punishment for the deliberate one and his sinfulness by saying: “So that he may taste the consequences of his deed. God has pardoned what is past. But whoever returns [to sin], God will take vengeance on him.” The Sunnah came from the rulings of the Prophet, may God bless him and grant him peace, and the rulings of his companions with the necessity of punishment for error, just as the Book indicates it for deliberate sin. Also, killing game is destruction, and destruction is guaranteed in deliberate and forgetful sins, but the deliberate one is sinful, and the mistaken one is not to be blamed. And the Almighty’s saying: Then the recompense is like that which he killed from the livestock, some of them read it with the addition, and others read it with its conjunction, The recompense is like that which he killed from the livestock, and Ibn Jarir narrated that Ibn Masoud read it, The recompense is like that which he killed from the livestock. And in his saying The recompense is like that which he killed from the livestock, according to both readings, there is evidence for what Malik, Al-Shafi’i, Ahmad and the majority went to, of the obligation of the recompense from like that which the pilgrim killed, if he had a similar animal from the domesticated animal, contrary to Abu Hanifa, may God have mercy on him, who obligated the value whether the killed game was of the same type or not. He said: He has the choice, if he wants to give its price in charity, or if he wants to buy an offering with it, and what the companions ruled regarding the like is more worthy of being followed, for they ruled in the case of an ostrich with a camel, and in the case of a wild cow with a cow, and in the case of a gazelle with a goat, and the mention of the companions’ rulings and their chains of transmission is established in the Book of Rulings. As for if the game was not of the same type, Ibn Abbas ruled in it with its price to be carried to Mecca, narrated by Al-Bayhaqi. God the Almighty said: Let it be judged by two just men among you meaning that two just men from among the Muslims judge with the penalty in the same amount or with the value in something other than the same amount. The scholars differed regarding the killer: Is it permissible for him to be one of the two judges? There are two opinions: One of them No, because he may be accused of his judgment against himself, and this is the school of Malik. The second Yes, due to the generality of the verse, and this is the school of Shafi’i and Ahmad. The first scholars argued that the judge cannot be judged in one case. Ibn Abi Hatim said: My father told us, Abu Nu’aym al-Fadl ibn Dukayn told us, Ja’far - he is Ibn Burqan - told us on the authority of Maymun ibn Mihran that a Bedouin came to Abu Bakr and said: I killed game while I was in a state of ihram, so what do you think is the penalty for me? Abu Bakr, may God be pleased with him, said to Ubayy ibn Ka’b while he was sitting with him: What do you think about what he said? The Bedouin said: I came to you while you were the successor of the Messenger of God, may God bless him and grant him peace, to ask you, but you are asking someone else? Abu Bakr said: What do you object to? God the Almighty says: Then the recompense is an equivalent of that which was killed from livestock, as judged by two just men among you. So I consulted my companion, and when we agreed on a matter, we ordered you to do it. This is a good chain of transmission, but it is interrupted between Maymun and As-Siddiq, and something similar is possible here. As-Siddiq explained the ruling to him gently and slowly, because he saw him as an ignorant Bedouin. The cure for ignorance is education. As for if the objector is attributed to knowledge, Ibn Jarir said: Hannad and Abu Hisham Al-Rafa’i told us: Waki’ bin Al-Jarrah told us, on the authority of Al-Mas’udi, on the authority of Abdul-Malik bin Umair, on the authority of Qubaysah bin Jabir, who said: We went out as pilgrims, and when we prayed the morning prayer, we would lead our mounts, and we would walk and talk. He said: While we were there one morning, a gazelle or a wild goat appeared before us, and a man who was with us threw a stone at it, but it did not miss its tibia which is the bone protruding behind the ear, so it mounted its back and died. He said: So we felt great sorrow for him, and when we arrived in Mecca, I went out with him until we came to Umar ibn al-Khattab, may God be pleased with him, and he told him the story. He said: And beside him was a man whose face was like a heart of silver, meaning Abd al-Rahman ibn Awf. Umar turned to his companion and spoke to him. He said: Then he turned to the man and said: Did you kill him intentionally or by mistake? The man said: I shot him intentionally and did not intend to kill him. Umar said: I see that you have combined intentional and accidental killing. Go to a sheep and slaughter it and give its meat in charity, and keep its hide. He said: So we got up from him, and I said to my companion: O man, honor the symbols of God. The Commander of the Faithful did not know what to give you until he asked his companion: Go to your she-camel and slaughter it. Perhaps that means that it will suffice for you. Qubaysah said: I do not remember the verse from Surat Al-Ma'idah It shall be judged by two just men among you. When Umar heard what I had said, he did not surprise us except with the whip. He said: My companion struck me with the whip. You killed in the sanctuary and made a foolish judgment. He said: Then he turned to me and I said: O Commander of the Faithful, I do not permit for you today anything that is forbidden to you from me. He said: O Qubaysah bin Jabir, I see that you are young in age, broad-minded, and eloquent. A young man may have nine good morals and one bad moral, but a bad moral corrupts the good morals. So beware of the stumbling blocks of youth. Hisham narrated this story on the authority of Abdul Malik bin Umair, on the authority of Qubaysah, in a similar manner. He also narrated it on the authority of Hisin, on the authority of Al-Sha’bi, on the authority of Qubaysah, in a similar manner. He mentioned it as a mursal on the authority of Umar bin Bakr bin Abdullah Al-Muzani and Muhammad bin Sirin in a similar manner. Ibn Jarir said: Ibn Bashar told us, Abdul Rahman told us, Shu’bah told us, on the authority of Mansur, on the authority of Abu Wa’il, Ibn Jarir Al-Bajali told me: I killed a gazelle while I was in a state of ihram, so I mentioned that to Umar, and he said: Go to two of your brothers and let them judge you. So I went to Abdul Rahman and Sa’d, and they judged me to be a black billy goat. Ibn Jarir said: Ibn Wakee’ told us, Ibn Uyaynah told us, on the authority of Mukhariq, on the authority of Tariq, who said: Arbad trampled on a gazelle and killed it while he was in a state of ihram. He came to Umar to pass judgment on him, but Umar said to him: Judge with me. So they ruled that he was a young goat that had gathered water and trees. Then Umar said: Two just men among you shall judge it. This indicates that the killer may be one of the two judges, as Ash-Shafi’i and Ahmad may God have mercy on them said. They differed: Should the government be renewed in everything that happens to a person in a state of ihram, so that two just men shall judge it, even if the Companions had already ruled in a similar case, or should the previous rulings of the Companions suffice? There are two opinions. Ash-Shafi’i and Ahmad said: What the Companions ruled should be followed in this, and they made it an established law that cannot be deviated from. If the Companions did not rule, then two just men should be referred to. Malik and Abu Hanifa said: Rather, a ruling must be made for each individual, whether the Companions had a ruling on the same matter or not, based on the statement of God the Almighty: Two just men among you shall judge it. God the Almighty said: As an offering reaching the Kaaba meaning reaching the Kaaba, and what is meant is its arrival at the Sacred Sanctuary by slaughtering it there and distributing its meat to the poor of the Sacred Sanctuary, and this is a matter agreed upon in this case. And His saying: Or an expiation by feeding the poor or the equivalent of that in fasting meaning if the pilgrim does not find the same amount of livestock as he killed, or the game killed was not of similar size, or we say that in this case there is a choice between the penalty, feeding, and fasting, as is the opinion of Malik, Abu Hanifah, Abu Yusuf, and Muhammad ibn al-Hasan, and one of the two opinions of al-Shafi’i, and the well-known opinion from Ahmad, may God have mercy on them, due to the apparent meaning of or as being for choice, and the other opinion is that it is in order, so the image of that is that it is adjusted to the value, so the game killed is valued according to Malik, Abu Hanifah and his companions, Hammad, and Ibrahim. Al-Shafi’i said: The equivalent of it in livestock is equivalent if it were available, then food is bought with it and given in charity, and a mudd of it is given to each poor person, according to Al-Shafi’i, Malik and the jurists of Hijaz, and Ibn Jarir chose it. Abu Hanifa and his companions said: Each poor person is fed a mudd, and this is the opinion of Mujahid. Ahmad said: A mudd of wheat or a mudd of something else. If he does not find any, or we say that it is optional, he fasts for each poor person one day. Ibn Jarir said: Others said: He fasts one day for each sa’ as in the punishment for the one who indulges in luxury by shaving and the like, for the Lawgiver ordered Ka’b ibn ‘Ujrah to divide the portion among six, or to fast for three days, and the portion is three sa’s. They differed about the place of this feeding, so Al-Shafi’i said: Its place is the Haram, and this is the opinion of ‘Ata’. Malik said: He feeds in the place where he hunted the game or the closest place to it. Abu Hanifa said: If he wishes, he may feed in the Haram, and if he wishes, he may feed elsewhere. Mentioning the sayings of the predecessors in this regard Ibn Abi Hatim said: My father told us, Yahya bin Al-Mughira told us, Jarir told us, on the authority of Mansur, on the authority of Al-Hakam, on the authority of Muqsim, on the authority of Ibn Abbas, regarding the words of God Almighty: “Then the penalty is an equivalent of what he killed of livestock, as judged by two just men among you, as an offering delivered to the Kaaba, or an expiation of feeding poor people, or the equivalent of that in fasting.” He said: If the pilgrim kills game, he is judged to be compensated for it in livestock. If he does not find any, he looks at its price, then he evaluates its price in food. God Almighty said: or an expiation of feeding poor people, or the equivalent of that in fasting. He said: What is meant by food and fasting is that if he finds food, he finds his penalty. Ibn Jarir narrated it on the authority of Jarir. Ali bin Abi Talha said on the authority of Ibn Abbas: A sacrificial animal that reaches the Kaaba or an expiation of feeding the poor or the equivalent of that in fasting. So if the pilgrim kills a game animal, he is judged for it. If he kills a gazelle or something similar, he must slaughter a sheep in Mecca. If he cannot find one, he must feed six poor people. If he cannot find one, he must fast for three days. If he kills a deer or something similar, he must give a cow. If he cannot find one, he must feed twenty poor people. If he cannot find one, he must fast for twenty days. If he kills an ostrich or a wild donkey or something similar, he must give a camel. If he cannot find one, he must feed thirty poor people. If he cannot find one, he must fast for thirty days.” Narrated by Ibn Abi Hatim and Ibn Jarir, and he added: The food is a measure of food that will satisfy them. Jabir al-Ja’fi said, on the authority of Amir al-Sha’bi, Ata’ and Mujahid, or the equivalent of that in fasting. They said that the food is only for those who do not reach the sacrificial animal. Narrated by Ibn Jarir. Ibn Jurayj also narrated on the authority of Mujahid and Asbat on the authority of al-Suddi that they are in order. Ata’, Ikrimah and Mujahid said in one narration: Ad-Dahhak and Ibrahim Al-Nakha’i: It is up to the choice, and it is the narration of Al-Layth on the authority of Mujahid, on the authority of Ibn Abbas, and Ibn Jarir, may God have mercy on him, chose that. And His statement, that he may taste the evil consequences of his deed, meaning, We made expiation obligatory upon him so that he may taste the punishment for his action in which he committed the transgression. God has pardoned what is past, meaning in the time of ignorance, for whoever did good in Islam and followed the law of God, and did not commit a sin. Then He said, But whoever returns [to sin], God will take vengeance upon him, meaning whoever does that after it was forbidden in Islam and the legal ruling reached him, then God will take vengeance upon him, and God is Exalted in Might and Possessor of Retribution. Ibn Jurayj said: I said to Ata’: What is God has pardoned what is past? He said: What was in ignorance? I said: What is But whoever returns [to sin], God will take vengeance upon him? He said: Whoever returns [to sin] in Islam, God will take vengeance upon him, and he must also pay expiation. I said: Is there a punishment for returning [to sin] that you know of? He said: No. I said: Do you think that the Imam has the right to punish him? He said: No, it is a sin that he committed between himself and God Almighty, but he can atone for it. Narrated by Ibn Jarir. It was said: Its meaning is that God will take revenge on him with expiation. This was said by Saeed bin Jubair and Ata’. Then the majority of the predecessors and successors are of the opinion that whenever a pilgrim kills game, the penalty is due, and there is no difference between the first, second, and third, even if what was repeated was repeated, whether it was by mistake or intentionally. Ali bin Abi Talha said on the authority of Ibn Abbas, who said: Whoever kills a game by mistake while in a state of ihram, he will be judged for it every time he kills it. If he kills it intentionally, he will be judged for it once. If he returns, it will be said to him: May God take revenge on you, as God the Almighty said. Ibn Jarir said: Amr bin Ali told us, Yahya bin Saeed and Ibn Abi Uday told us, all on the authority of Hisham, who is Ibn Hassan, on the authority of Ikrimah, on the authority of Ibn Abbas, regarding whoever kills a game that is judged for him and then returns, he said: He will not be judged, God will take revenge on him. This is what Shuraih, Mujahid, Saeed bin Jubayr, Al-Hasan Al-Basri and Ibrahim Al-Nakha’i said, and Ibn Jarir narrated them, then he chose the first statement. Ibn Abi Hatim said: Al-Abbas bin Yazid Al-Abdi told us, Al-Mu’tamir bin Sulayman told us on the authority of Zaid bin Abi Al-Mu’alla, on the authority of Al-Hasan Al-Basri that a man killed a game and passed it by, then he returned and killed another game, so a fire came down from the sky and burned it. This is what God said: And whoever returns, God will take revenge on him. Ibn Jarir said about his statement, And God is Exalted in Might and Possessor of Retribution, He, may His remembrance be glorified, says: God is impregnable in His dominion, no one can subdue Him, and no one can prevent Him from taking revenge on whomever He takes revenge on, nor can anyone prevent Him from punishing whomever He wants to punish, because creation is His creation, and the command is His command, and He has might and protection. And His statement, Possessor of Retribution, means that He is the One who punishes whoever disobeys Him for his disobedience to Him.
5:95: Al-Walibi said on the authority of Ibn Abbas, regarding his statement, God will surely test you with something of the game that your hands and spears may reach, he said: It is the weak and small game that God tests His servants with during their state of ihram, to the point that if they wanted to, they could reach it with their hands, but God forbade them from approaching it. Mujahid said, That your hands may reach, meaning the small and fledgling game, and your spears, meaning the large ones. Muqatil ibn Hayyan said: This verse was revealed during the Umrah of Hudaybiyyah, when wild animals, birds and game would overtake them in their camps, something they had never seen before. So God forbade them from killing it while they were in a state of ihram, so that God may know who fears Him unseen. That is, God Almighty tests them with game, which would overtake them in their camps, so that they could seize it with their hands and spears, secretly and openly, so that the obedience of those who obey them in secret and openly would be apparent, as God Almighty said: Indeed, those who fear their Lord unseen will have forgiveness and a great reward. And His statement here, But whoever transgresses after that, Al-Suddi and others said: meaning after this notification, warning and advance, he will have a painful punishment, that is, for disobeying God’s command and law. Then God the Almighty said: O you who believe! Do not kill game while you are in a state of ihram. This is a prohibition from God the Almighty to kill game while in a state of ihram, and a prohibition against engaging in it while in a state of ihram. This only includes, in terms of meaning, edible game and what is born from it and other things. As for non-edible land animals, according to al-Shafi’i, it is permissible for the person in a state of ihram to kill them, and the majority of scholars are of the opinion that it is also forbidden to kill them. No exception is made to this except what is proven in the two Sahihs on the authority of al-Zuhri on the authority of Urwah, on the authority of Aisha, the Mother of the Believers, that the Messenger of God, may God bless him and grant him peace, said: “Five pests are to be killed in the sanctuary and outside of it: the crow, the kite, the scorpion, the mouse, and the rabid dog.” Malik said, on the authority of Nafi’, on the authority of Ibn Umar: The Messenger of God, may God bless him and grant him peace, said: “Five pests are to be killed in the sanctuary and outside of it: the crow, the kite, the scorpion, the mouse, and the rabid dog.” Narrated by both of them, and Ayoub narrated it on the authority of Nafi’ on the authority of Ibn Umar in a similar manner. Ayoub said: So I said to Nafi’: What about the snake? He said: There is no doubt about the snake. There is no disagreement about killing it. Some scholars, such as Malik and Ahmad, include the wolf, the wild beast, the tiger, and the cheetah with the rabid dog, because they are more harmful than it. And God knows best. Zayd ibn Aslam and Sufyan ibn Uyaynah said: The rabid dog includes all of these wild beasts. Those who said this supported their argument with what was narrated that when the Messenger of God (peace and blessings of God be upon him) supplicated against Utbah ibn Abi Lahab, he said: O God, let Your dog in Ash-Sham rule over him, and the wild beast ate him in Zarqa. They said: If he kills anything other than them, he must pay its ransom, such as the hyena, the fox, the wild cat, and the like. Malik said: The young ones of these five stipulated are also excluded from this, as well as the young ones of the wild beasts that are included in them. Al-Shafi’i said: It is permissible for the pilgrim to kill everything whose meat is not eaten, and there is no difference between young and old ones. He made the general reason that they are not eaten. Abu Hanifa said: The pilgrim must kill the rabid dog and the wolf, because they are wild dogs. If he kills something other than them, he must pay its ransom, unless another wild beast attacks it and kills it, in which case he does not have to pay ransom. This is the opinion of Al-Awza’i and Al-Hasan ibn Salih ibn Hayy. Zafar ibn Al-Hudhayl said: He must pay ransom for anything other than that, even if it attacks him. Some people said: What is meant by the crow here is the spotted crow, which is the one with white on its belly and back but not on its armor, which is black, and the a’sam, which is the white, based on what was narrated by An-Nasa’i on the authority of Amr ibn Ali Al-Fallas, on the authority of Yahya Al-Qattan, on the authority of Shu’bah, on the authority of Qatadah, on the authority of Sa’id ibn Al-Musayyab, on the authority of Aishah, on the authority of the Prophet, may God bless him and grant him peace, who said: “There are five things that a person in ihram may kill: a snake, a mouse, a kite, a spotted crow, and a rabid dog.” The majority are of the opinion that what is meant by it is more general than that, based on what was proven in the two Sahihs of its general wording. Malik, may God have mercy on him, said: A person in ihram may not kill a crow unless it attacks him and harms him. Mujahid ibn Jabr and a group said: He should not kill it, but rather throw it away. The same was narrated on the authority of Ali. Hisham narrated: Yazid ibn Abi Ziyad told us, on the authority of Abd Al-Rahman ibn Abi Na’im, on the authority of Abu Sa’id, on the authority of the Prophet, may God bless him and grant him peace, that he was asked about what a person in ihram may kill? He said: The snake, the scorpion, the mousetrap, the crow that shoots but does not kill it, the rabid dog, the kite, and the wild beast. Narrated by Abu Dawud on the authority of Ahmad ibn Hanbal, and al-Tirmidhi on the authority of Ahmad ibn Mani’, both on the authority of Hisham, and Ibn Majah on the authority of Abu Karim and on the authority of Muhammad ibn Fadil, both on the authority of Yazid ibn Abi Ziyad, and it is weak because of it. Al-Tirmidhi said: This is a good hadith. And the Almighty said: And whoever among you kills it intentionally, the penalty is an equivalent of what he killed from livestock. Ibn Abi Hatim said: Abu Saeed Al-Ashj narrated to us, Ibn Ulayyah narrated to us from Ayoub, who said: I was told from Tawus that he said: The penalty is not imposed on the one who kills game by mistake, rather the penalty is imposed on the one who kills it deliberately. This is a strange opinion from Tawus, and he adheres to the apparent meaning of the verse. Mujahid bin Jabr said: What is meant by the intentional here is the one who intends to kill the game, forgetting his state of ihram. As for the one who intentionally kills the game while remembering his state of ihram, then his matter is greater than that he should make expiation, and his state of ihram is invalidated. Ibn Jarir narrated it from him through the chain of transmission of Ibn Abi Nujayh, Layth bin Abi Sulaym and others from him, and it is also a strange opinion. What the majority are of the opinion is that the one who kills intentionally and the one who forgets are equal in the obligation of the penalty upon him. Al-Zuhri said: The Book indicates the deliberate one, and the Sunnah indicates the forgetful one. The meaning of this is that the Qur’an indicates the necessity of punishment for the deliberate one and his sinfulness by saying: “So that he may taste the consequences of his deed. God has pardoned what is past. But whoever returns [to sin], God will take vengeance on him.” The Sunnah came from the rulings of the Prophet, may God bless him and grant him peace, and the rulings of his companions with the necessity of punishment for error, just as the Book indicates it for deliberate sin. Also, killing game is destruction, and destruction is guaranteed in deliberate and forgetful sins, but the deliberate one is sinful, and the mistaken one is not to be blamed. And the Almighty’s saying: Then the recompense is like that which he killed from the livestock, some of them read it with the addition, and others read it with its conjunction, The recompense is like that which he killed from the livestock, and Ibn Jarir narrated that Ibn Masoud read it, The recompense is like that which he killed from the livestock. And in his saying The recompense is like that which he killed from the livestock, according to both readings, there is evidence for what Malik, Al-Shafi’i, Ahmad and the majority went to, of the obligation of the recompense from like that which the pilgrim killed, if he had a similar animal from the domesticated animal, contrary to Abu Hanifa, may God have mercy on him, who obligated the value whether the killed game was of the same type or not. He said: He has the choice, if he wants to give its price in charity, or if he wants to buy an offering with it, and what the companions ruled regarding the like is more worthy of being followed, for they ruled in the case of an ostrich with a camel, and in the case of a wild cow with a cow, and in the case of a gazelle with a goat, and the mention of the companions’ rulings and their chains of transmission is established in the Book of Rulings. As for if the game was not of the same type, Ibn Abbas ruled in it with its price to be carried to Mecca, narrated by Al-Bayhaqi. God the Almighty said: Let it be judged by two just men among you meaning that two just men from among the Muslims judge with the penalty in the same amount or with the value in something other than the same amount. The scholars differed regarding the killer: Is it permissible for him to be one of the two judges? There are two opinions: One of them No, because he may be accused of his judgment against himself, and this is the school of Malik. The second Yes, due to the generality of the verse, and this is the school of Shafi’i and Ahmad. The first scholars argued that the judge cannot be judged in one case. Ibn Abi Hatim said: My father told us, Abu Nu’aym al-Fadl ibn Dukayn told us, Ja’far - he is Ibn Burqan - told us on the authority of Maymun ibn Mihran that a Bedouin came to Abu Bakr and said: I killed game while I was in a state of ihram, so what do you think is the penalty for me? Abu Bakr, may God be pleased with him, said to Ubayy ibn Ka’b while he was sitting with him: What do you think about what he said? The Bedouin said: I came to you while you were the successor of the Messenger of God, may God bless him and grant him peace, to ask you, but you are asking someone else? Abu Bakr said: What do you object to? God the Almighty says: Then the recompense is an equivalent of that which was killed from livestock, as judged by two just men among you. So I consulted my companion, and when we agreed on a matter, we ordered you to do it. This is a good chain of transmission, but it is interrupted between Maymun and As-Siddiq, and something similar is possible here. As-Siddiq explained the ruling to him gently and slowly, because he saw him as an ignorant Bedouin. The cure for ignorance is education. As for if the objector is attributed to knowledge, Ibn Jarir said: Hannad and Abu Hisham Al-Rafa’i told us: Waki’ bin Al-Jarrah told us, on the authority of Al-Mas’udi, on the authority of Abdul-Malik bin Umair, on the authority of Qubaysah bin Jabir, who said: We went out as pilgrims, and when we prayed the morning prayer, we would lead our mounts, and we would walk and talk. He said: While we were there one morning, a gazelle or a wild goat appeared before us, and a man who was with us threw a stone at it, but it did not miss its tibia which is the bone protruding behind the ear, so it mounted its back and died. He said: So we felt great sorrow for him, and when we arrived in Mecca, I went out with him until we came to Umar ibn al-Khattab, may God be pleased with him, and he told him the story. He said: And beside him was a man whose face was like a heart of silver, meaning Abd al-Rahman ibn Awf. Umar turned to his companion and spoke to him. He said: Then he turned to the man and said: Did you kill him intentionally or by mistake? The man said: I shot him intentionally and did not intend to kill him. Umar said: I see that you have combined intentional and accidental killing. Go to a sheep and slaughter it and give its meat in charity, and keep its hide. He said: So we got up from him, and I said to my companion: O man, honor the symbols of God. The Commander of the Faithful did not know what to give you until he asked his companion: Go to your she-camel and slaughter it. Perhaps that means that it will suffice for you. Qubaysah said: I do not remember the verse from Surat Al-Ma'idah It shall be judged by two just men among you. When Umar heard what I had said, he did not surprise us except with the whip. He said: My companion struck me with the whip. You killed in the sanctuary and made a foolish judgment. He said: Then he turned to me and I said: O Commander of the Faithful, I do not permit for you today anything that is forbidden to you from me. He said: O Qubaysah bin Jabir, I see that you are young in age, broad-minded, and eloquent. A young man may have nine good morals and one bad moral, but a bad moral corrupts the good morals. So beware of the stumbling blocks of youth. Hisham narrated this story on the authority of Abdul Malik bin Umair, on the authority of Qubaysah, in a similar manner. He also narrated it on the authority of Hisin, on the authority of Al-Sha’bi, on the authority of Qubaysah, in a similar manner. He mentioned it as a mursal on the authority of Umar bin Bakr bin Abdullah Al-Muzani and Muhammad bin Sirin in a similar manner. Ibn Jarir said: Ibn Bashar told us, Abdul Rahman told us, Shu’bah told us, on the authority of Mansur, on the authority of Abu Wa’il, Ibn Jarir Al-Bajali told me: I killed a gazelle while I was in a state of ihram, so I mentioned that to Umar, and he said: Go to two of your brothers and let them judge you. So I went to Abdul Rahman and Sa’d, and they judged me to be a black billy goat. Ibn Jarir said: Ibn Wakee’ told us, Ibn Uyaynah told us, on the authority of Mukhariq, on the authority of Tariq, who said: Arbad trampled on a gazelle and killed it while he was in a state of ihram. He came to Umar to pass judgment on him, but Umar said to him: Judge with me. So they ruled that he was a young goat that had gathered water and trees. Then Umar said: Two just men among you shall judge it. This indicates that the killer may be one of the two judges, as Ash-Shafi’i and Ahmad may God have mercy on them said. They differed: Should the government be renewed in everything that happens to a person in a state of ihram, so that two just men shall judge it, even if the Companions had already ruled in a similar case, or should the previous rulings of the Companions suffice? There are two opinions. Ash-Shafi’i and Ahmad said: What the Companions ruled should be followed in this, and they made it an established law that cannot be deviated from. If the Companions did not rule, then two just men should be referred to. Malik and Abu Hanifa said: Rather, a ruling must be made for each individual, whether the Companions had a ruling on the same matter or not, based on the statement of God the Almighty: Two just men among you shall judge it. God the Almighty said: As an offering reaching the Kaaba meaning reaching the Kaaba, and what is meant is its arrival at the Sacred Sanctuary by slaughtering it there and distributing its meat to the poor of the Sacred Sanctuary, and this is a matter agreed upon in this case. And His saying: Or an expiation by feeding the poor or the equivalent of that in fasting meaning if the pilgrim does not find the same amount of livestock as he killed, or the game killed was not of similar size, or we say that in this case there is a choice between the penalty, feeding, and fasting, as is the opinion of Malik, Abu Hanifah, Abu Yusuf, and Muhammad ibn al-Hasan, and one of the two opinions of al-Shafi’i, and the well-known opinion from Ahmad, may God have mercy on them, due to the apparent meaning of or as being for choice, and the other opinion is that it is in order, so the image of that is that it is adjusted to the value, so the game killed is valued according to Malik, Abu Hanifah and his companions, Hammad, and Ibrahim. Al-Shafi’i said: The equivalent of it in livestock is equivalent if it were available, then food is bought with it and given in charity, and a mudd of it is given to each poor person, according to Al-Shafi’i, Malik and the jurists of Hijaz, and Ibn Jarir chose it. Abu Hanifa and his companions said: Each poor person is fed a mudd, and this is the opinion of Mujahid. Ahmad said: A mudd of wheat or a mudd of something else. If he does not find any, or we say that it is optional, he fasts for each poor person one day. Ibn Jarir said: Others said: He fasts one day for each sa’ as in the punishment for the one who indulges in luxury by shaving and the like, for the Lawgiver ordered Ka’b ibn ‘Ujrah to divide the portion among six, or to fast for three days, and the portion is three sa’s. They differed about the place of this feeding, so Al-Shafi’i said: Its place is the Haram, and this is the opinion of ‘Ata’. Malik said: He feeds in the place where he hunted the game or the closest place to it. Abu Hanifa said: If he wishes, he may feed in the Haram, and if he wishes, he may feed elsewhere. Mentioning the sayings of the predecessors in this regard Ibn Abi Hatim said: My father told us, Yahya bin Al-Mughira told us, Jarir told us, on the authority of Mansur, on the authority of Al-Hakam, on the authority of Muqsim, on the authority of Ibn Abbas, regarding the words of God Almighty: “Then the penalty is an equivalent of what he killed of livestock, as judged by two just men among you, as an offering delivered to the Kaaba, or an expiation of feeding poor people, or the equivalent of that in fasting.” He said: If the pilgrim kills game, he is judged to be compensated for it in livestock. If he does not find any, he looks at its price, then he evaluates its price in food. God Almighty said: or an expiation of feeding poor people, or the equivalent of that in fasting. He said: What is meant by food and fasting is that if he finds food, he finds his penalty. Ibn Jarir narrated it on the authority of Jarir. Ali bin Abi Talha said on the authority of Ibn Abbas: A sacrificial animal that reaches the Kaaba or an expiation of feeding the poor or the equivalent of that in fasting. So if the pilgrim kills a game animal, he is judged for it. If he kills a gazelle or something similar, he must slaughter a sheep in Mecca. If he cannot find one, he must feed six poor people. If he cannot find one, he must fast for three days. If he kills a deer or something similar, he must give a cow. If he cannot find one, he must feed twenty poor people. If he cannot find one, he must fast for twenty days. If he kills an ostrich or a wild donkey or something similar, he must give a camel. If he cannot find one, he must feed thirty poor people. If he cannot find one, he must fast for thirty days.” Narrated by Ibn Abi Hatim and Ibn Jarir, and he added: The food is a measure of food that will satisfy them. Jabir al-Ja’fi said, on the authority of Amir al-Sha’bi, Ata’ and Mujahid, or the equivalent of that in fasting. They said that the food is only for those who do not reach the sacrificial animal. Narrated by Ibn Jarir. Ibn Jurayj also narrated on the authority of Mujahid and Asbat on the authority of al-Suddi that they are in order. Ata’, Ikrimah and Mujahid said in one narration: Ad-Dahhak and Ibrahim Al-Nakha’i: It is up to the choice, and it is the narration of Al-Layth on the authority of Mujahid, on the authority of Ibn Abbas, and Ibn Jarir, may God have mercy on him, chose that. And His statement, that he may taste the evil consequences of his deed, meaning, We made expiation obligatory upon him so that he may taste the punishment for his action in which he committed the transgression. God has pardoned what is past, meaning in the time of ignorance, for whoever did good in Islam and followed the law of God, and did not commit a sin. Then He said, But whoever returns [to sin], God will take vengeance upon him, meaning whoever does that after it was forbidden in Islam and the legal ruling reached him, then God will take vengeance upon him, and God is Exalted in Might and Possessor of Retribution. Ibn Jurayj said: I said to Ata’: What is God has pardoned what is past? He said: What was in ignorance? I said: What is But whoever returns [to sin], God will take vengeance upon him? He said: Whoever returns [to sin] in Islam, God will take vengeance upon him, and he must also pay expiation. I said: Is there a punishment for returning [to sin] that you know of? He said: No. I said: Do you think that the Imam has the right to punish him? He said: No, it is a sin that he committed between himself and God Almighty, but he can atone for it. Narrated by Ibn Jarir. It was said: Its meaning is that God will take revenge on him with expiation. This was said by Saeed bin Jubair and Ata’. Then the majority of the predecessors and successors are of the opinion that whenever a pilgrim kills game, the penalty is due, and there is no difference between the first, second, and third, even if what was repeated was repeated, whether it was by mistake or intentionally. Ali bin Abi Talha said on the authority of Ibn Abbas, who said: Whoever kills a game by mistake while in a state of ihram, he will be judged for it every time he kills it. If he kills it intentionally, he will be judged for it once. If he returns, it will be said to him: May God take revenge on you, as God the Almighty said. Ibn Jarir said: Amr bin Ali told us, Yahya bin Saeed and Ibn Abi Uday told us, all on the authority of Hisham, who is Ibn Hassan, on the authority of Ikrimah, on the authority of Ibn Abbas, regarding whoever kills a game that is judged for him and then returns, he said: He will not be judged, God will take revenge on him. This is what Shuraih, Mujahid, Saeed bin Jubayr, Al-Hasan Al-Basri and Ibrahim Al-Nakha’i said, and Ibn Jarir narrated them, then he chose the first statement. Ibn Abi Hatim said: Al-Abbas bin Yazid Al-Abdi told us, Al-Mu’tamir bin Sulayman told us on the authority of Zaid bin Abi Al-Mu’alla, on the authority of Al-Hasan Al-Basri that a man killed a game and passed it by, then he returned and killed another game, so a fire came down from the sky and burned it. This is what God said: And whoever returns, God will take revenge on him. Ibn Jarir said about his statement, And God is Exalted in Might and Possessor of Retribution, He, may His remembrance be glorified, says: God is impregnable in His dominion, no one can subdue Him, and no one can prevent Him from taking revenge on whomever He takes revenge on, nor can anyone prevent Him from punishing whomever He wants to punish, because creation is His creation, and the command is His command, and He has might and protection. And His statement, Possessor of Retribution, means that He is the One who punishes whoever disobeys Him for his disobedience to Him.
5:96: Ibn Abi Talha said, on the authority of Ibn Abbas in a narration on his authority, and Saeed bin Al-Musayyab, and Saeed bin Jubair and others, in the words of God Almighty: Lawful to you is the game of the sea meaning what is caught from it fresh and its food what is provided from it sweet and dry, and Ibn Abbas said in the famous narration on his authority: Its game is what is taken from it alive and its food is what is thrown out dead, and thus it was narrated on the authority of Abu Bakr Al-Siddiq, Zaid bin Thabit, Abdullah bin Amr, Abu Ayyub Al-Ansari, may God be pleased with them, and Ikrimah, Abu Salamah bin Abdul Rahman, Ibrahim Al-Nakha’i, and Al-Hasan Al-Basri. Sufyan bin Uyaynah said, on the authority of Amr bin Dinar, on the authority of Ikrimah, on the authority of Abu Bakr Al-Siddiq that he said its food is everything in it, narrated by Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim, and Ibn Jarir said: Ibn Hamid told us, Jarir told us on the authority of Mughirah, on the authority of Samak, who said: I was told on the authority of Ibn Abbas, who said: Abu Bakr addressed the people and said: Lawful to you is the game of the sea And its food is for your enjoyment.” And its food is what it throws up. He said: Ibn Ulayyah told us on the authority of Sulayman al-Taymi, on the authority of Abu Majlaz, on the authority of Ibn Abbas, regarding his statement, Lawful to you is the game of the sea and its food, he said, its food is what it throws up. Akrima said on the authority of Ibn Abbas, he said: His food is what he expels from dead animals, and Ibn Jarir also narrated it. Saeed bin Al-Musayyab said: His food is what he expels alive or rolls up and dies, narrated by Ibn Abi Hatim. Ibn Jarir said: Ibn Bashar told us, Abdul Wahhab told us, Ayoub told us on the authority of Nafi’ that Abdul Rahman bin Abi Hurairah asked Ibn Umar, saying: The sea has thrown up many dead whales, so can we eat them? He said: Do not eat them. When Abdullah returned to his family, he took the Qur’an and read Surat Al-Ma’idah and came to this verse: And his food is provision for you and for the travelers, and he said: Go and tell him: Let him eat it, for it is his food. Ibn Jarir chose this way, that what is meant by his food is what died in it. A report has been narrated on this matter, although some of them narrate it as a narration that ends with the Prophet. Hannad bin Al-Sarri told us: Abdah bin Sulayman told us, on the authority of Muhammad bin Amr, Abu Salamah told us, on the authority of Abu Hurayrah, who said: The Messenger of God, may God bless him and grant him peace, said: Lawful to you is the game of the sea and its food as provision for you. He said: Its food is that which it throws up dead. Then he said: Some of them stopped this hadith with Abu Hurayrah. Hannad told us, Ibn Abi Zaydah told us, on the authority of Muhammad bin Amr, on the authority of Abu Salamah, on the authority of Abu Hurayrah, regarding his statement: Lawful to you is the game of the sea and its food, he said: Its food is that which it throws up dead. His saying, Provision for you and for the travelers, meaning benefit and sustenance for you, O you who are being addressed, and for the travelers, which is the plural of siyar. Ikrimah said: for those who are in the presence of the sea and traveling. Another said: the fresh part of it is for those who hunt it from the presence of the sea, and its food is what dies in it or is caught from it, salted and dried, as provisions for travelers and those far from the sea. Something similar was narrated from Ibn Abbas, Mujahid, and al-Suddi and others. The majority have proven the permissibility of his death by this noble verse, and by what Imam Malik bin Anas narrated on the authority of Ibn Wahb and Ibn Kaysan, on the authority of Jabir bin Abdullah, who said: The Messenger of God, may God bless him and grant him peace, sent an expedition towards the coast, and he put Abu Ubaidah bin Al-Jarrah in charge of them, and they were three hundred, and I was among them. He said: So we set out until we were on the way, and the provisions ran out, so Abu Ubaidah ordered the provisions of that army, and he gathered all of it, and my provisions were dates. He said: Our sustenance was little by little every day until it ran out, and we were only getting one date at a time, so he said: We found its loss when it ran out. He said: Then we reached the sea and there was a fish like a humpback, and that army ate from it for eighteen nights, then Abu Ubaidah ordered two of its ribs to be set up, then he ordered a camel to be mounted and it passed under them, but it did not reach them. This hadith is reported in the two Sahihs and it has chains of transmission on the authority of Jabir. In Sahih Muslim, on the authority of Abu al-Zubayr, on the authority of Jabir, “There was something like a huge sand dune on the shore of the sea. We came to it and there was a beast called al-Anbar.” Abu Ubaidah said: It is dead. Then he said: “No, we are messengers of the Messenger of God, may God bless him and grant him peace, and you are forced to eat.” He said: “So we stayed with him for a month, and we were three hundred until we became fat. I saw us scooping up fat from the hollows of his eyes with jugs, and he cut off from it the udder like a bull.” He said: “Abu Ubaidah took thirteen men from us and made them sit in the hollows of his eyes, and he took one of his ribs and made it stand up, then he saddled the largest camel with us, and it passed under it, and we took provisions from its meat and meat sha’iq. When we arrived in Madinah, we came to the Messenger of God, may God bless him and grant him peace, and we mentioned that to him, and he said: “It is a provision that God has brought forth for you. Do you have any of its meat with you so that you can feed us?” He said: “So we sent some to the Messenger of God, may God bless him and grant him peace, and he ate it.” In some of the narrations of Muslim, they were with the Prophet, may God bless him and grant him peace, when they found this fish. Some of them said: It is another incident. Some of them said: Rather, it is one incident, but they were with the Prophet, may God bless him and grant him peace, first, then he sent them on a raid with Abu Ubaidah and they found this in their raid with Abu Ubaidah. And God knows best. Malik said on the authority of Safwan bin Saleem on the authority of Saeed bin Salamah from the family of Ibn Al-Azraq: Al-Mughirah bin Abi Burdah, who was from Banu Abd Al-Dar, told him that he heard Abu Hurairah say: A man asked the Messenger of God, may God bless him and grant him peace, and said: O Messenger of God, we travel by sea and carry a little water with us, and if we perform ablution with it we become thirsty. Can we perform ablution with seawater? The Messenger of God, may God bless him and grant him peace, said: Its water is pure and its dead are lawful. This hadith was narrated by the two Imams Al-Shafi’i and Ahmad bin Hanbal and the people of the four Sunans, and it was authenticated by Al-Bukhari, Al-Tirmidhi, Ibn Hibban and others. It was narrated on the authority of a group of the Companions on the authority of the Prophet, may God bless him and grant him peace, in a similar manner. Imam Ahmad, Abu Dawud, Al-Tirmidhi and Ibn Majah narrated through various chains of transmission on the authority of Hammad ibn Salamah, who said: Abu Al-Muhazzam - he is Yazid ibn Sufyan - told us: I heard Abu Hurairah say: We were with the Messenger of God, may God bless him and grant him peace, during Hajj or Umrah, and we encountered locusts, so we began to hit them with our sticks and whips, killing them. We lost hope, so we said: What should we do while we are in ihram? So we asked the Messenger of God, may God bless him and grant him peace, and he said: There is nothing wrong with hunting at sea. Abu Al-Muhazzam is weak, and God knows best. Ibn Majah said: Harun bin Abdullah al-Jammal told us, Hashim bin al-Qasim told us, Ziyad bin Abdullah told us, on the authority of Allam, on the authority of Musa bin Muhammad bin Ibrahim, on the authority of his father, on the authority of Jabir and Anas bin Malik that when the Prophet, may God bless him and grant him peace, used to supplicate against locusts, he would say: O God, destroy their adults, kill their young, spoil their eggs, cut off their roots, and seize their mouths from our livelihoods and provisions, for You are the Hearer of supplications. Khalid said: O Messenger of God, how can you supplicate against one of God’s soldiers to cut off their roots? He said: The locusts are the scatter of the whale in the sea. Hashim said: Ziyad said: I was told by someone who saw the whale scatter them, and this is unique to Ibn Majah. Al-Shafi’i narrated on the authority of Sa’id, on the authority of Ibn Jurayj, on the authority of Ata’, on the authority of Ibn Abbas, that he denounced those who hunt locusts in the Haram. This noble verse was used as evidence by those jurists who believed that sea creatures may be eaten, and they did not exclude anything from that. It was previously reported on the authority of As-Siddiq that he said: Its food is everything in it. Some of them excluded frogs and permitted everything else, based on what Imam Ahmad, Abu Dawud and An-Nasa’i narrated on the authority of Ibn Abi Dhi’b, on the authority of Sa’id ibn Khalid, on the authority of Sa’id ibn Al-Musayyab, on the authority of Abdur-Rahman ibn Uthman At-Taymi, that the Messenger of God, may God bless him and grant him peace, forbade the killing of frogs. An-Nasa’i narrated on the authority of Abdullah ibn Amr, who said: The Messenger of God, may God bless him and grant him peace, forbade the killing of frogs, and said: Its croaking is glorification of God. Others said: Fish may be eaten from sea catch, but frogs may not be eaten. They differed concerning other than them. It was said: All of that may be eaten. It was said: It may not be eaten. It was said: Whatever is similar to it on land is similar to it in the sea. What is not eaten is similar to what is not eaten. These are all aspects of the Shafi’i school of thought, may God Almighty have mercy on him. A similar hadith has been reported. Then he narrated it through the path of Ismail ibn Umayya and Yahya ibn Abi Anisa, on the authority of Abu al-Zubayr, on the authority of Jabir, and it is rejected. The majority of the companions of Malik, al-Shafi’i, and Ahmad ibn Hanbal used as evidence the hadith of ambergris mentioned above, and the hadith: Its water is pure and its dead are permissible, which has also been mentioned. Imam Abu Abdullah Al-Shafi’i narrated on the authority of Abd Al-Rahman bin Zaid bin Aslam, on the authority of his father, on the authority of Ibn Umar, who said: The Messenger of God, may God bless him and grant him peace, said: “Two dead things and two types of blood have been made lawful for us. As for the two dead things, they are fish and locusts, and as for the two types of blood, they are the liver and the spleen.” It was narrated by Ahmad, Ibn Majah, Al-Darqutni, and Al-Bayhaqi, and it has corroborating evidence. It was narrated as a narration that ends with the Prophet, and God knows best. And his saying, And hunting on land is forbidden to you as long as you are in a state of ihram, meaning while you are in a state of ihram, hunting is forbidden to you. This indicates that this is forbidden. So if a person in a state of ihram hunts game intentionally, he has sinned and will pay, or by mistake, he will pay and it is forbidden for him to eat it, because in his case it is like a dead animal, and likewise in the case of others in a state of ihram or in a state of ihram, according to Malik and al-Shafi’i in one of his two opinions, and this is what ‘Ata’, al-Qasim, Salim, Abu Sayf, Muhammad ibn al-Hasan and others say. If he eats it or part of it, is he required to pay a second penalty? There are two opinions of the scholars regarding this. One of them Yes, Abd al-Razzaq said, on the authority of Ibn Jurayj, on the authority of ‘Ata’ who said: If he slaughters it and then eats it, then there are two expiations, and this is the opinion of a group. The second There is no penalty for eating it, as Malik ibn Anas stated. Abu Omar bin Abdul Barr said: This is the opinion of the jurists of the regions and the majority of scholars. Then Abu Omar directed him to the case of someone who had intercourse, then had intercourse, then had intercourse before he was punished, then he is only subject to one punishment. Abu Hanifa said: He is subject to the value of what he ate. Abu Thawr said: If the pilgrim kills game, he is liable for its punishment and it is permissible to eat that game, except that I dislike it for the one who killed it, based on the hadith from the Messenger of God, may God bless him and grant him peace: Game of the land is permissible for you, and you are in a state of ihram, unless you hunt it or it is hunted for you. This hadith will be explained, and his statement that it is permissible for the killer is strange. As for others, there is a difference of opinion about it, and we have mentioned the prohibition from those who came before. Others said that it is permissible for someone other than the killer, whether those in a state of ihram or those who are in a state of ihram, based on this hadith, and God knows best. If a lawful person hunts game and gives it to a person in ihram, some scholars have permitted it absolutely, and they did not question whether he hunted it for it or not. This statement was narrated by Abu Omar bin Abdul Barr, on the authority of Omar bin Al-Khattab, Abu Hurairah, Al-Zubayr bin Al-Awwam, Kaab Al-Ahbar, Mujahid, and Ata’ in one narration, and Saeed bin Jubair. The Kufians also said the same. Ibn Jarir said: Muhammad bin Abdullah bin Buzaie’ told us, Bishr bin Al-Fadl told us, Saeed told us, on the authority of Qatadah, that Saeed bin Al-Musayyab told him, on the authority of Abu Hurairah, that he was asked about the meat of game hunted by a lawful person, can a person in ihram eat it? He said: So he gave them a fatwa to eat it, then he met Omar bin Al-Khattab and told him what had happened, and he said: If you had given them a fatwa other than this, I would have given you a headache. Others said: It is not permissible for a person in ihram to eat game at all, and they forbade it absolutely due to the generality of this noble verse. Abdul Razzaq said on the authority of Muammar, on the authority of Ibn Tawus, and Abdul Karim on the authority of Ibn Abi Asiya, on the authority of Tawus, on the authority of Ibn Abbas that he disliked eating game for the person in ihram, and he said: It is ambiguous, meaning his statement, And forbidden to you is the game of land as long as you are in ihram. He said: Muammar informed me on the authority of Al-Zuhri, on the authority of Ibn Umar, that he disliked for the person in ihram to eat the meat of game under all circumstances. Muammar said: Ayoub informed me on the authority of Nafi’, on the authority of Ibn Umar, something similar. Ibn Abd Al-Barr said: Tawus and Jabir bin Zaid said the same, and Al-Thawri and Ishaq bin Rahawayh agreed with it in one narration. Something similar was narrated on the authority of Ali bin Abi Talib, narrated by Ibn Jarir on the authority of Saeed bin Abi Arubah, on the authority of Qatadah, on the authority of Saeed bin Al-Musayyab that Ali disliked eating the meat of game for the person in ihram under all circumstances. Malik, Ash-Shafi’i, Ahmad ibn Hanbal, Ishaq ibn Rahawayh in one narration, and the majority of scholars said: If the halal person intended to hunt it, the muhrim is not permitted to eat it, based on the hadith of As-Sa’ib ibn Jaththama, who gave the Prophet (peace and blessings of God be upon him) a wild donkey while he was in Abwa’ or Budan, so he returned it to him. When he saw the look on his face, he said, We did not return it to you except because we are forbidden. This hadith is narrated in the two Sahihs, and it has many different wordings. They said: The reason for it is that the Prophet (peace and blessings of God be upon him) thought that he had hunted it for his own sake, so he returned it for that reason. However, if he did not intend to hunt it, then it is permissible for him to eat from it, based on the hadith of Abu Qatadah, who hunted a wild donkey, and it was halal, not forbidden, and his companions were in a state of ihram. They hesitated about eating it, then they asked the Messenger of God (peace and blessings of God be upon him), and he said, Was there anyone among you who pointed to it or helped in killing it? They said, No. He said, Then eat from it. The Messenger of God (peace and blessings of God be upon him) ate from it. This story is also proven in the two Sahihs with many different wordings. Imam Ahmad said: Saeed bin Mansour and Qutaybah bin Saeed told us: Yaqoub bin Abdul Rahman told us, on the authority of Amr bin Abi Amr, on the authority of Al-Muttalib bin Abdullah bin Hantab, on the authority of Jabir bin Abdullah, who said: The Messenger of God, may God bless him and grant him peace, said, and Qutaybah said in his hadith: I heard the Messenger of God, may God bless him and grant him peace, say: Game of the land is lawful for you. Saeed said - and you are in a state of ihram - as long as you do not hunt it or it is hunted for you. And this is how Abu Dawud, Al-Tirmidhi and Al-Nasa’i narrated it, all on the authority of Qutaybah. Al-Tirmidhi said: We do not know of Al-Muttalib hearing it from Jabir. Imam Muhammad bin Idris Al-Shafi’i, may God be pleased with him, narrated it on the authority of Amr bin Abi Amr, on the authority of his client Al-Muttalib, on the authority of Jabir, then he said: This is the best hadith narrated on this topic and the most reasonable. Malik, may God be pleased with him, said: on the authority of Abdullah bin Abi Bakr. On the authority of Abdullah bin Aamer bin Rabia, he said: I saw Uthman bin Affan in Al-Arj while he was in the state of ihram on a summer day, and he had covered his face with a purple blanket. Then some game meat was brought to him and he said to his companions: Eat. They said: Will you not eat yourself? He said: I am not like you, it was hunted for my sake.
